JSON: Name: competence_iceberg_model_development Title: Mixed-methods development and psychometric validation of a competence-iceberg measurement model for academic medical postgraduates Short Hypothesis: A five-factor competence-iceberg model derived from behavioral event interviews and refined via expert consultation will produce a measurement scale that demonstrates acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha ≥ 0.80), convergent validity (AVE > 0.50, CR ≥ 0.80), and acceptable confirmatory factor analysis fit (χ2/df < 3, CFI ≥ 0.90, RMSEA ≤ 0.08) when administered to academic medical postgraduates. Related Work: Existing competence frameworks in medical education emphasize clinical competencies, milestone-based assessment, or generalized professional roles; some frameworks target physician-scientists or specialty training but are mainly expert-driven and focused on observable performance indicators (e.g., publications, clinical skills). Prior measurement efforts have concentrated on clinical competence scales, nurse specialist competency instruments, and role-based competency lists; few instruments target academic medical postgraduates or combine qualitative item generation with rigorous psychometric validation. Limitations in current approaches include (1) emphasis on surface performance rather than latent competence constructs, (2) reliance on expert opinion without mixed-methods item derivation, (3) weak or incomplete psychometric validation (limited EFA/CFA, AVE/CR reporting, or cross-validation), and (4) contextual bias from clinical-orientation and country-specific graduation requirements, which reduces suitability for assessing research-oriented postgraduate competence. Abstract: This project addresses the lack of validated tools for measuring core competencies of academic medical postgraduates by developing and validating a competence-iceberg model and corresponding measurement scale. We propose a mixed-methods pipeline: behavioral event interviews for item generation, iterative expert consultation for content validity, and quantitative validation through exploratory factor analysis and confirmatory factor analysis on independent samples. The main contribution is a rigorously derived five-factor model (cooperation and communication, experimental/research, academic performance, learning and ethical adherence, and practical ability) with an associated scale tested for internal consistency, convergent/discriminant validity, and structural fit. Expected outcomes are a psychometrically sound instrument and an empirically grounded competence-iceberg framework that enable multidimensional assessment of academic medical postgraduates and support curriculum design, targeted feedback, and future longitudinal research into competence development. Experiments: Dataset: multi-center cross-sectional survey of academic medical postgraduates and mentors from ≥5 universities; target N ≥ 600 valid responses; split random subsamples: EFA sample n ≈ 0.5N, CFA sample n ≈ 0.5N; pilot sample n ≈ 150 for initial item testing. Item generation: behavioral event interviews with purposive sample of mentors and postgraduates (audio-recorded, transcribed) and two rounds of expert consultation producing final item pool (~26 items). Baselines: (a) adapted ACGME/Vanderbilt competency constructs (aggregated score), (b) existing clinical competency scales relevant to postgraduate assessment. Evaluation metrics: (1) Content validity indices (I-CVI, UA-CVI, Ave-CVI), (2) EFA: KMO, Bartlett’s test, item communalities, eigenvalues>1, varimax rotation, factor loadings ≥ 0.40, explained variance target ≥ 60%, (3) Internal consistency: Cronbach’s alpha per factor and total (≥0.80), (4) Convergent validity: AVE ≥ 0.50, CR ≥ 0.80, (5) Discriminant validity: square root(AVE) > inter-factor correlations, (6) CFA: χ2/df < 3, CFI ≥ 0.90, TLI ≥ 0.90, RMSEA ≤ 0.08, SRMR ≤ 0.08, (7) Test-retest reliability: ICC ≥ 0.70 on subsample after 2–4 weeks, (8) Criterion validity: Pearson/Spearman correlations and regression models predicting objective academic outcomes (number of publications, grant awards, academic honors). Experimental setup: (1) Pilot administration and item analysis; remove items with communalities < 0.40 or cross-loadings; (2) EFA on first subsample to extract factor structure; compute factor scores; (3) CFA on second subsample to confirm structure and compute fit indices; (4) Measurement invariance tests across subgroups (degree type, year, gender) using multi-group CFA (configural, metric, scalar); (5) Predictive validity: hierarchical regression of objective outcomes using baseline scales and new factor scores to test incremental validity; (6) Ablation studies: (a) remove each factor sequentially and re-evaluate model fit and predictive power, (b) remove items with top/bottom 10% item-total correlations to quantify impact on reliability and AVE, (c) compare full instrument vs. reduced instruments (e.g., performance-only items) on explained variance of academic outcomes. Statistical thresholds: use two-tailed tests with α = 0.05 and report 95% confidence intervals; adjust for multiple comparisons when applicable. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sample and generalization: sample restricted to China and predominantly master’s students may limit external validity and cross-cultural generalizability. Response bias: social desirability and mentor-influenced responses may inflate self-reported competence. Construct coverage: items influenced by local publication/graduation requirements may overweight academic performance relative to other competencies. Measurement failure modes: factor cross-loadings, low communalities, or model non-identification in CFA; insufficient sample size for stable multi-group invariance testing. Predictive validity limits: short-term cross-sectional design limits ability to predict long-term career outcomes. Statistical and computational constraints: large sample and multi-group CFA require substantial compute and expertise; small subgroup sizes may preclude reliable invariance tests. Ceiling/floor effects: highly skewed item responses (e.g., universally high self-ratings) may reduce discriminative power. Operational limitations: reliance on self-report rather than objective behavioral tasks may limit ecological validity and inflate correlations due to common-method variance.
